question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=3.$ Given that the point $P(3,3,-3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-2$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(3,3).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(3,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(3,3) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(3,3) & ={f}_{y}(3,3)(y-(3)) \\ z-(-3) & =(-2)(y-(3)) \\ z-(-3) & =6 - 2 y \\ z & =3 - 2 y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(3,3,-3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{x=3 \\ z=3 - 2 y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3 - 2 y$ (or $- 2 y - z + 3=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j - 2 k \\  & =⟨0,1,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

$$

$$

- For the plane $z=3 x + 2$ (or $3 x - z + 2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

$$
